evidence: Many students mistakenly believe that all metals are magnetic, but this is not true; gold, silver, and copper do not respond to magnets.
q: Riya holds a magnet near a copper coin and an iron nail. What will happen?
options: Only the iron nail is pulled to the magnet
Both the coin and the nail are pulled
Neither moves unless the magnet is rubbed first
The nail moves only if it is a magnet
explain: Magnets pull iron, nickel and cobalt, but copper, gold and silver do not respond to magnets.

wrong.text: Both the coin and the nail are pulled
wrong.why: thinks all metals are magnetic

wrong.text: Neither moves unless the magnet is rubbed first
wrong.why: confuses magnetism with static electricity

wrong.text: The nail moves only if it is a magnet
wrong.why: thinks only magnets are attracted

evidence: A common observation is that a magnet attracts an iron nail, but this does not mean the nail has become a magnet itself; it is simply being pulled by the magnetic field.
q: A magnet picks up an iron nail. What does this tell us about the nail?
options: It is only pulled, not made a magnet
It has turned into a magnet itself
It is stuck to the magnet like glue
It has been charged with static electricity
explain: The nail is simply pulled by the magnetic field; being attracted does not make it a magnet.

wrong.text: It has turned into a magnet itself
wrong.why: thinks anything attracted must be a magnet

wrong.text: It is stuck to the magnet like glue
wrong.why: thinks magnets work like glue

wrong.text: It has been charged with static electricity
wrong.why: confuses magnetism with static electricity

evidence: If you test a bar magnet, you will find that the magnetic force is concentrated at the two ends, known as poles, rather than at the center.
q: Iron pins are sprinkled along a bar magnet. Where will most pins stick?
options: At the two ends of the magnet
In the middle of the magnet
Spread evenly along the whole magnet
Only at the end marked North
explain: The magnetic force is concentrated at the two poles at the ends, not at the centre.

wrong.text: In the middle of the magnet
wrong.why: thinks the centre is strongest

wrong.text: Spread evenly along the whole magnet
wrong.why: thinks the force is the same everywhere

wrong.text: Only at the end marked North
wrong.why: thinks only the North pole attracts

evidence: Dropping a magnet, hammering it, or heating it to high temperatures can actually damage its internal structure and weaken its force.
q: Arjun's old magnet has become weak. Which is the most likely reason?
options: It was dropped or heated many times
Its power was used up over the years
It was not heated enough to stay strong
Its sticky surface has worn off
explain: Magnets keep their magnetism unless mishandled; dropping, hammering or heating damages them and weakens their force.

wrong.text: Its power was used up over the years
wrong.why: thinks magnets run down like batteries

wrong.text: It was not heated enough to stay strong
wrong.why: thinks heat makes magnets stronger

wrong.text: Its sticky surface has worn off
wrong.why: thinks magnets work like glue

evidence: This line only bisects the chord if it is perpendicular to it; a random line from the centre does not guarantee bisection.
q: A line from the centre of a circle meets a chord. When does it cut the chord into equal halves?
options: Only when it is perpendicular to the chord
Always, because it starts from the centre
Only when the chord passes near the middle
Only when the circle is large enough
explain: A line from the centre bisects a chord only if it is perpendicular to the chord.

wrong.text: Always, because it starts from the centre
wrong.why: thinks any line from the centre bisects a chord

wrong.text: Only when the chord passes near the middle
wrong.why: mixes this up with the longest chord

wrong.text: Only when the circle is large enough
wrong.why: thinks size changes the rule

evidence: Third, remember that the angle in a semicircle is always 90 degrees, forming a right-angled triangle regardless of whether the triangle is isosceles or scalene.
q: AB is a diameter and C is a point on the circle, so ABC is scalene. What is angle ACB?
options: It is exactly 90 degrees
Less than 90, as it is not isosceles
It depends on the circle's radius
It is exactly 180 degrees
explain: The angle in a semicircle is always 90 degrees, whether the triangle is isosceles or scalene.

wrong.text: Less than 90, as it is not isosceles
wrong.why: thinks the rule needs an isosceles triangle

wrong.text: It depends on the circle's radius
wrong.why: thinks the angle changes with size

wrong.text: It is exactly 180 degrees
wrong.why: mixes it up with opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral

evidence: Finally, note that a cyclic quadrilateral must have its four vertices on the circle, and its opposite angles must sum to 180 degrees, not be equal to each other.
q: In a cyclic quadrilateral, one angle is 70 degrees. What is the angle opposite to it?
options: 110 degrees
70 degrees
90 degrees
290 degrees
explain: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees, so the other angle is 110 degrees.

wrong.text: 70 degrees
wrong.why: thinks opposite angles are equal

wrong.text: 90 degrees
wrong.why: mixes it up with the angle in a semicircle

wrong.text: 290 degrees
wrong.why: subtracts from a full turn of 360 degrees

evidence: These officers were assigned 'jagirs', which were revenue-collecting areas, but they did not own the land; they could only collect taxes, and they were frequently transferred to prevent them from becoming too powerful.
q: Why were mansabdars moved from one jagir to another so often?
options: To stop them from becoming too powerful
So they could rule each area like a king
Because jagirs were gifts they had to share
So they could count elephants in each area
explain: Mansabdars only collected taxes from jagirs and were transferred often so that none became too powerful.

wrong.text: So they could rule each area like a king
wrong.why: thinks mansabdars ruled their jagirs

wrong.text: Because jagirs were gifts they had to share
wrong.why: thinks jagirs were permanent gifts of land

wrong.text: So they could count elephants in each area
wrong.why: thinks rank was about owning animals

evidence: Officers known as mansabdars held a 'zat' rank, which determined their personal status and salary, rather than the number of animals they owned.
q: Two mansabdars have different zat ranks. What does that difference tell you?
options: Which one had higher status and salary
Which one owned more elephants
Which one owned more land as a gift
Which one was the emperor's eldest son
explain: The zat rank decided an officer's personal status and salary, not how many animals he owned.

wrong.text: Which one owned more elephants
wrong.why: thinks zat counted animals

wrong.text: Which one owned more land as a gift
wrong.why: thinks jagirs were land they owned

wrong.text: Which one was the emperor's eldest son
wrong.why: thinks rank came from birth order

evidence: While the Emperor appointed many officials, local hereditary landlords called zamindars often acted as intermediaries to collect revenue from peasants.
q: How was a zamindar different from an officer sent by the Emperor?
options: He was a local landlord by birth
He was an official appointed from Delhi
He owned and ruled a whole jagir
He ran the zabt survey everywhere
explain: Zamindars were local hereditary landlords who collected revenue, not officials sent by the Emperor.

wrong.text: He was an official appointed from Delhi
wrong.why: thinks zamindars were Mughal officials

wrong.text: He owned and ruled a whole jagir

evidence: Furthermore, Akbar’s policy of 'sulh-i kul' or 'universal peace' was not a new religion, but a philosophy of tolerance that allowed people of different faiths to coexist peacefully in his empire.
q: What did Akbar's policy of sulh-i kul ask people in his empire to do?
options: Live in peace alongside other faiths
Join a new religion made by Akbar
Follow only the emperor's own faith
Pay one equal tax in every region
explain: Sulh-i kul meant universal peace: tolerance that let people of different faiths live together, not a new religion.

wrong.text: Join a new religion made by Akbar
wrong.why: thinks sulh-i kul was a new religion

wrong.text: Follow only the emperor's own faith
wrong.why: thinks tolerance meant one faith for all

wrong.text: Pay one equal tax in every region

evidence: Contrary to common belief, its dark colour is primarily due to the presence of deep basaltic lava rocks and high clay content, rather than high organic humus levels.
q: A soil sample is very dark but has little humus. How can this be?
options: Its lava rock and clay make it dark
It must have humus hidden deep inside
The water it stores makes it look dark
It was burnt black by forest fires
explain: Black soil is dark mainly because of basaltic lava rocks and clay, not because of humus.

wrong.text: It must have humus hidden deep inside
wrong.why: thinks dark soil always means humus

wrong.text: The water it stores makes it look dark
wrong.why: links the colour to holding water

wrong.text: It was burnt black by forest fires
wrong.why: guesses from everyday experience of black ash

evidence: While it is most extensive in the Northern Plains, our map analysis showed it is also found in the eastern coastal plains, particularly in the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri rivers.
q: A farmer lives in the Godavari delta. Which soil do his fields most likely have?
options: Alluvial soil, as in the Northern Plains
Black soil, as on lava plateaus
Not alluvial, since that is only in the north
Laterite soil, because of heavy rain

wrong.text: Black soil, as on lava plateaus

wrong.text: Not alluvial, since that is only in the north

wrong.text: Laterite soil, because of heavy rain

evidence: We learned that while human actions like overgrazing and deforestation accelerate the process, natural forces like wind and flowing water are equally significant agents of erosion.
q: If no people lived on a hilly area, would its soil still erode?
options: Yes, wind and running water still erode it
No, only people cause soil erosion
No, erosion needs grazing animals to start
Yes, but only by wind on flat land
explain: Wind and flowing water are equally important agents of erosion, so soil erodes even without people.

wrong.text: No, only people cause soil erosion
wrong.why: thinks erosion is only caused by humans

wrong.text: No, erosion needs grazing animals to start

wrong.text: Yes, but only by wind on flat land
wrong.why: thinks erosion is only wind across flat land

evidence: I used to think coal was made from dead dinosaurs, but she explained that coal actually formed from the burial of large land plants in swampy areas millions of years ago.
q: Ravi says coal comes from dinosaur bones. Which fact from the lesson shows he is wrong?
options: Coal formed from large plants buried in swamps
Dinosaurs lived only in swampy areas
Coal is trapped in rock pores with oil
Coal can be made in a laboratory
explain: Coal formed from large land plants buried in swamps millions of years ago, not from dinosaurs.

Yes, with the right heat in a few days

evidence: Many students thought it was just filtering out dirt, but it is actually a complex process of fractional distillation to separate various useful components.

Dirt and sand are filtered out of it
All of it is turned into petrol
It is mixed with coal tar for roads
explain: Refining is fractional distillation, which separates petroleum into useful products like paraffin wax, not just filtering dirt.

wrong.text: All of it is turned into petrol
